"I owe my family and all of you an apology," Jensen Huang wrote. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." Huang added that he'd "fallen short" of his responsibility to the company. "To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me," he said. The investigation will be conducted by independent directors working with outside legal counsel. extraction.body: Nvidia has opened an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. U.S. intelligence agencies have expressed concerns that the woman, Alice Huang, who is affiliated with a cloud company and an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, has been passing information to Beijing, according to reports in The New York Times and the Financial Times. Huang told Nvidia staff in an email on Sunday that he had an affair with the woman and that Nvidia's board of directors had opened an independent investigation into the spying allegations. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang wrote in the message. "I am deeply sorry." An Nvidia spokesperson said that Huang was committed to continuing as CEO of Nvidia without interruption. In a statement, the Nvidia board said it would investigate the allegations that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," Nvidia's board said in a statement. Read Huang's email to Nvidia employees and the company board of directors' statement here . The allegations come as Nvidia has become the center of a trade dispute between China and the U.S. as AI is seen as increasingly critical to national security. The U.S. restricts exports of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips to China, though it has approved exports of certain older, slower models. Megaspeed, which Ms. Huang is affiliated with, has been accused of helping restricted Chinese companies acquire Nvidia AI chips. Nvidia representatives previously said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls. Nvidia's Huang has pushed for broader AI chip exports to China, saying it is better for the U.S. if the world uses and builds on American technology. He has also aligned with President Donald Trump on American artificial intelligence policy and its infrastructure buildout. In his note to staff, Huang said he was "proud and grateful" to be an American. Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Huang on Wednesday asking him to sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18. Nvidia reports third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17 and will hold a major conference in Washington, D.C., at the end of the month. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you. sources.title: US markets open as tech giant Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy - BBC
passages: US tech giant Nvidia has announced it is launching an independent investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang, over reports he had an affair with Alice Huang - who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.
The man in question, Jensen Huang, says he has "fallen short" of his responsibility to serve his colleagues, in a statement shared with Nvidia staff.
He tells Radio 4's Today programme that it "would not be beyond the Chinese state" to threaten sending Huang's family to prison were she not to co-operate, now she was in a position to do so.
The company suffered a sharp drop in pre-market trading, but the full extent of how damaging the revelations about Huang’s affair looks will become clear now regular trading has begun.
Donald Trump says Huang is "a fine person, but you never know what's going on" , while the Chinese government says the claims are nothing more than a " smear intended to malign China "
Nvidia designs some of the most sophisticated AI chips on the planet - and since 2022 the US has used various export controls to keep its top tech out of China
Both US and China can win in AI, Huang tells BBC in 2025

extraction.body: Nvidia has opened an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. U.S. intelligence agencies have expressed concerns that the woman, Alice Huang, who is affiliated with a cloud company and an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, has been passing information to Beijing, according to reports in The New York Times and the Financial Times. Huang told Nvidia staff in an email on Sunday that he had an affair with the woman and that Nvidia's board of directors had opened an independent investigation into the spying allegations. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang wrote in the message. "I am deeply sorry." An Nvidia spokesperson said that Huang was committed to continuing as CEO of Nvidia without interruption. In a statement, the Nvidia board said it would investigate the allegations that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," Nvidia's board said in a statement. Read Huang's email to Nvidia employees and the company board of directors' statement here . The allegations come as Nvidia has become the center of a trade dispute between China and the U.S. as AI is seen as increasingly critical to national security. The U.S. restricts exports of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips to China, though it has approved exports of certain older, slower models. Megaspeed, which Ms. Huang is affiliated with, has been accused of helping restricted Chinese companies acquire Nvidia AI chips. Nvidia representatives previously said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls. Nvidia's Huang has pushed for broader AI chip exports to China, saying it is better for the U.S. if the world uses and builds on American technology. He has also aligned with President Donald Trump on American artificial intelligence policy and its infrastructure buildout. In his note to staff, Huang said he was "proud and grateful" to be an American. Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Huang on Wednesday asking him to sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18. passages: US tech giant Nvidia has announced it is launching an independent investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang, over reports he had an affair with Alice Huang - who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.
The man in question, Jensen Huang, says he has "fallen short" of his responsibility to serve his colleagues, in a statement shared with Nvidia staff.
He tells Radio 4's Today programme that it "would not be beyond the Chinese state" to threaten sending Huang's family to prison were she not to co-operate, now she was in a position to do so.
The company suffered a sharp drop in pre-market trading, but the full extent of how damaging the revelations about Huang’s affair looks will become clear now regular trading has begun.
Donald Trump says Huang is "a fine person, but you never know what's going on" , while the Chinese government says the claims are nothing more than a " smear intended to malign China "

passages: Nvidia’s board of directors announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation .

In response to earlier reports about the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, Nvidia had said that the pair’s interactions were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with customers.
As the AI race between the United States and China heats up , chips, especially Nvidia’s chips, have been a major focus .
A memo circulating among U.S. policymakers earlier this year claimed that Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Jensen Huang wrote.
“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” he said.

Nvidia also published a message that Huang sent to the company admitting that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed (though he didn’t mention her by name). A memo circulating among U.S. policymakers earlier this year claimed that Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Jensen Huang wrote. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang added that he’d “fallen short” of his responsibility to the company. “To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” he said. As the AI race between the United States and China heats up , chips, especially Nvidia’s chips, have been a major focus . Huang also seems to have a close relationship with President Donald Trump , who’s been a cheerleader of the AI ( or “superintelligence” ) industry. In its announcement, Nvidia’s board said that it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or company secrets were compromised. It also said that Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” and that the board has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.” The investigation will be conducted by independent directors working with outside legal counsel. extraction.body: US tech giant Nvidia is opening a probe into its CEO, Jensen Huang, after reports that Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort," the company's board of directors announced on Sunday. A report by The New York Times said that the CEO had admitted to the board that he had been "unfaithful" with a business executive who, according to US intelligence, was gathering information for China. Nvidia is one of the global leaders in the development of artificial intelligence. Its chips power many of the data centres and computing systems used to train and run AI models. Its advanced chips have also been targeted by US export restrictions to prevent China from getting the latest semiconductor technology. In a letter addressed to Nvidia employees, Huang said that he took "full responsibility" for his actions, while admitting to being unfaithful to his wife and apologising to his family and colleagues. However, he did not mention the name of the person involved or her reported ties to Beijing. "Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life," the 63-year-old wrote. "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility." China has consistantly rejected the spying allegations, with foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun telling a regular briefing on Monday that "the narrative of a so-called Chinese spy is entirely baseless vilification and smearing." China rejects report of spy plot targeting Nvidia's Jensen Huang The board leading the company, which is one of the most valuable in the world, says it has "no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia's secrets were compromised, but that a thorough independent investigation would be carried out. The board added that Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it." In his letter to employees, Jensen Huang said, "I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security." George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, told AFP that "it would be premature to conclude that Jensen poses a threat to US national security before the facts are fully established." "Once you become famous, you will naturally become a target," Chen said. "The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised." Last month, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies had discovered that Huang had developed close ties with Chinese citizen and chip buyer Alice Huang, and that she was directly sharing information with Beijing. Alice Huang is a top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that runs data centres across Southeast Asia and has become Nvidia's largest customer in the region. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump was asked on Sunday whether he should have acted on the spying information sooner. However, Trump praised Huang, saying, "I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. He's done an amazing job for our country." Trump is heading to the Asia-Pacific summit in China's Shenzhen next week and told reporters Huang is invited, saying: "I don't know but I'll certainly take him."

sources.title: Is Jensen Huang’s job on the line? Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimates it’s “about a 50-50”
passages: The question is whether Huang can survive this.

To think through what could come next, this editor spoke Sunday with famed professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which has hosted Huang at its CEO summits.
Sonnenfeld likes Huang, he said, and he called Huang’s career salvageable but put the odds at “about a 50-50.” He also had a lot more food for thought.
Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang told staff he was unfaithful to his wife.
Sonnenfeld noted that Huang’s constant, public advocacy for selling advanced chips to China had already made people anxious.
But if Huang had one, Sonnenfeld continued, removing him would be harder.
Huang may well survive the investigation (Sonnenfeld hopes the board clears him of knowingly aiding anyone).
Sonnenfeld suggested that Huang’s saving grace could be what social psychologists call idiosyncrasy credits , if he can prove he was being duped.
Sonnenfeld expects that even if Huang keeps the title, he’ll have to hand off some of the day-to-day decision-making.

And boards in crisis often reach for a “messianic solution” from outside, Sonnenfeld said, floating former Google CEO Eric Schmidt as one idea. Huang doesn’t own the kind of super-voting stock that would cement his power at Nvidia. Sonnenfeld often argues for dual-class structures that empower founders, and he says Huang’s success without one has been the best counterargument to that case. But if Huang had one, Sonnenfeld continued, removing him would be harder. This episode may be remembered as a pivotal moment for how the tech industry guards its secrets. Sonnenfeld argues tech has been “way too lax” compared with defense contractors that face clearance regimes. The arrest last month of an OpenAI engineer points to the same problem. He was accused of hiding a recording device behind a TV in an executive conference room, and while OpenAI has said it has no indication that model weights, source code, or customer data were accessed, the case highlights how exposed tech companies are to people who get close. Huang may well survive the investigation (Sonnenfeld hopes the board clears him of knowingly aiding anyone). The bigger test comes when Nvidia’s employees, customers and partners, and, indirectly, the millions of Americans with Nvidia in their 401(k) plans, have to decide whether an AI economy built largely on the judgment of Huang still makes sense. extraction.body: Jensen Huang's three-decade reign atop Nvidia hangs in the balance as the chipmaker's board investigates the CEO's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Yale leadership expert Jeffrey Sonnenfeld puts Huang's survival odds at roughly 50-50, marking the most serious threat yet to the architect of the AI boom. The probe follows revelations that China's Ministry of State Security targeted Huang through a tech executive with close personal ties. Nvidia's board has launched an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang over his relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, plunging the world's most valuable chipmaker into a leadership crisis that could reshape the AI industry. Yale School of Management's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, who advises boards on CEO succession, told TechCrunch he estimates it's "about a 50-50" chance Huang remains in his role. The investigation follows a bombshell US intelligence memo revealing that China's Ministry of State Security recruited a tech executive to cultivate a relationship with Huang and gather intelligence on the CEO who controls the chips powering the global AI race. The suspected operative maintained what sources described as a close personal relationship with Huang, raising questions about potential security breaches at a company whose technology the US government considers critical to national security. Huang has led Nvidia since co-founding the company in 1993, steering it from a graphics card maker into a $3 trillion colossus that supplies the GPUs behind ChatGPT, Claude, and virtually every major AI system. His signature leather jacket and technical evangelism made him the face of the AI revolution, but that 33-year tenure now faces its gravest test. Sonnenfeld's 50-50 assessment carries weight. He runs Yale's Chief Executive Leadership Institute and has counseled boards through crises at companies from Boeing to Wells Fargo. The company controls roughly 80% of the AI accelerator market, with customers including OpenAI, Meta, Google, and Microsoft all dependent on its H100 and H200 chips. Just days before the investigation became public, Nvidia announced partnerships with Samsung and Korean firms on factory-floor AI deployments and opened its NVLink platform to Korean companies building sovereign AI infrastructure. The Chinese espionage angle adds another layer of complexity to Nvidia's already fraught relationship with Beijing. US export controls have banned the company from selling its most advanced chips to China, yet investigations found Nvidia's H200 chips reached Chinese buyers through a ghost company the Commerce Department had approved despite the firm operating from empty offices. The board now must weigh whether Huang's relationship with the suspected operative compromised the company's compliance with those restrictions or exposed sensitive technology. Industry insiders say the board faces an impossible calculus. He personally designed the company's strategy of betting on parallel processing years before AI made GPUs indispensable. He negotiated the deals that made Nvidia the sole supplier to virtually every AI lab. Analysts estimate his leadership added over $2 trillion to the company's market capitalization in the past two years alone. But the national security implications of a CEO potentially compromised by Chinese intelligence could force the board's hand regardless of Huang's value. The investigation comes as cybersecurity experts warn AI is ushering in a "dark age" for digital defenses, with AI-powered attacks overwhelming traditional security measures. The suspected espionage operation against Huang represents exactly the kind of sophisticated influence campaign that blends personal relationships with intelligence gathering, making it difficult to detect and even harder to defend against. Nvidia hasn't publicly commented on the investigation's timeline or scope. The company's board includes former executives from Google, Cisco, and the semiconductor industry, giving it deep technical expertise but also close ties to the same tech ecosystem that depends on Nvidia's continued stability. If the board determines Huang must step aside, the company has no obvious successor. Unlike Apple, which has groomed internal candidates for years, Nvidia's leadership structure revolves entirely around its founder. Investors are watching for any sign of how the investigation might resolve. Nvidia's stock has become a proxy for AI sentiment across the market, with its quarterly earnings moving the entire tech sector. A forced CEO transition would trigger questions about deal continuity, product roadmap execution, and whether Nvidia can maintain its technological edge without the visionary who created it. The 50-50 odds Sonnenfeld cited suggest even experts can't predict which way the board will break. The investigation into Jensen Huang represents more than a corporate governance crisis - it's a potential inflection point for the entire AI industry. If Nvidia's board decides the national security risks outweigh Huang's irreplaceable expertise, the company that makes AI possible will have to reinvent itself without the founder who built it. The next few weeks will determine whether the AI boom continues under Huang's leadership or enters a new, uncertain chapter.

Its advanced chips have also been targeted by US export restrictions to prevent China from getting the latest semiconductor technology. However, he did not mention the name of the person involved or her reported ties to Beijing. "Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life," the 63-year-old wrote. "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility." China has consistantly rejected the spying allegations, with foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun telling a regular briefing on Monday that "the narrative of a so-called Chinese spy is entirely baseless vilification and smearing." I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security." George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, told AFP that "it would be premature to conclude that Jensen poses a threat to US national security before the facts are fully established." "Once you become famous, you will naturally become a target," Chen said. "The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised." Alice Huang is a top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that runs data centres across Southeast Asia and has become Nvidia's largest customer in the region. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump was asked on Sunday whether he should have acted on the spying information sooner. However, Trump praised Huang, saying, "I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. He's done an amazing job for our country." Trump is heading to the Asia-Pacific summit in China's Shenzhen next week and told reporters Huang is invited, saying: "I don't know but I'll certainly take him."

extraction.body: Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang told staff he was unfaithful to his wife. But this isn’t a case of just another CEO having an extramarital affair. The romantic interest is Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy who was feeding information back to Beijing. In short, the stakes reach well beyond Nvidia, given how many tech and financial partners depend on its place at the center of the AI economy. “I’m responsible for an entire industry ,” Huang recently told Bloomberg in a sit-down. A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations in late October as “ groundless smears and slanders ,” and no one has been charged. But U.S. intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Donald Trump about their concerns a year ago, and unnamed senior officials inside the Trump administration told the Times that they doubt Huang could have remained unaware all that time of Alice Huang’s intelligence-gathering role for China. When Trump was first briefed, the Times reported, officials didn’t believe Huang knew, and it isn’t clear whether their assessment has changed. The board, meanwhile, says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised. The question is whether Huang can survive this. To think through what could come next, this editor spoke Sunday with famed professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which has hosted Huang at its CEO summits. Sonnenfeld likes Huang, he said, and he called Huang’s career salvageable but put the odds at “about a 50-50.” He also had a lot more food for thought. First, the damage. Until now, Huang has been “revered and trusted by everybody in technology,” Sonnenfeld noted. But he called this episode “remarkably poor judgment.” Even if Huang was merely naive, he said, “any employee in Nvidia other than him would be fired over this,” and the recklessness alone would mean “an irretrievable loss of confidence.” Sonnenfeld suggested that Huang’s saving grace could be what social psychologists call idiosyncrasy credits , if he can prove he was being duped. The term comes from Edwin Hollander, a social psychologist who proposed in a 1958 paper that people earn latitude in a group by showing competence and following its rules. Huang has been earning latitude since he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. But all that goodwill can run out when a screw-up looks self-serving or touches the group’s core norms. Here that group includes Nvidia’s board, its roughly 42,000 employees who are bound by security rules, and, in a looser sense, the U.S. government, given it restricts its exports. We also talked about precedents, except, as it turns out, there really are none for what’s unfolding right now. Executives who survive personal scandals sometimes pick up where they left off at another company, Sonnenfeld observed. Former HP CEO Mark Hurd is one example. Between 2005 and 2010, he drove HP to the top of the tech industry by revenue, then was pressured to resign after he filed inaccurate expense reports that hid a personal relationship with a contractor. Oracle hired him about a month later. Huang has no equivalent because Nvidia is his company As for the bench at Nvidia, that doesn’t really exist either. While there is typically a hierarchy inside companies of Nvidia’s scale and importance, Huang has kept things as flat as possible, with about 60 direct reports by his own account. That structure makes it hard to figure out who would succeed him (though his children, both of whom work at Nvidia, are sometimes the subject of succession speculation ). That won’t stop the worldwide guessing game that’s sure to follow. And boards in crisis often reach for a “messianic solution” from outside, Sonnenfeld said, floating former Google CEO Eric Schmidt as one idea. Nvidia’s role at the center of a massive and complex circular financing web is what makes this particular predicament so tricky and, undoubtedly, terrifying for a wide number of constituents. Nvidia isn’t just the biggest provider of chips driving the AI boom but also largely the bank behind the buildout. In addition to stakes in hundreds of smaller startups, Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave and Nebius. In August, it also signed preliminary agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion over time, and Huang has said Nvidia could backstop up to a quarter of it. The move was widely interpreted as a way to spread risk. Still, a leadership crisis at the center is how a stumble becomes a collapse. So what’s Nvidia’s board likely doing right now? Sonnenfeld noted that Huang’s constant, public advocacy for selling advanced chips to China had already made people anxious. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, whose company Nvidia has backed, had a lot to say about selling chips to China at Davos back in January, likening it to “ selling nuclear weapons to North Korea .” Now the board’s independent members — meaning everyone but Huang — will have to establish what technology reached China if any, and by what routes, including by better understanding Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed. The Singapore cloud company, which grew out of a Chinese gaming business and became Nvidia’s largest buyer in Southeast Asia, bought roughly $2 billion of its chips , the New York Times reported in October 2025, raising broader questions about whether it was helping China circumvent U.S. export restrictions by re-exporting the chips to China or renting them to Chinese customers remotely. (An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill after the Times report that the allegations were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year .”) In the meantime, Huang will keep running the company, Nvidia said Sunday. That’ll be a tall order, even for a CEO who already spends much of his time traveling the world to promote Nvidia. For starters, three House chairmen want a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18. Nvidia is also reporting its newest earnings on November 17. Sonnenfeld expects that even if Huang keeps the title, he’ll have to hand off some of the day-to-day decision-making. Only one thing is certain right now. Huang doesn’t own the kind of super-voting stock that would cement his power at Nvidia. Sonnenfeld often argues for dual-class structures that empower founders, and he says Huang’s success without one has been the best counterargument to that case. But if Huang had one, Sonnenfeld continued, removing him would be harder. This episode may be remembered as a pivotal moment for how the tech industry guards its secrets. Sonnenfeld argues tech has been “way too lax” compared with defense contractors that face clearance regimes. The arrest last month of an OpenAI engineer points to the same problem. He was accused of hiding a recording device behind a TV in an executive conference room, and while OpenAI has said it has no indication that model weights, source code, or customer data were accessed, the case highlights how exposed tech companies are to people who get close. Huang may well survive the investigation (Sonnenfeld hopes the board clears him of knowingly aiding anyone). The bigger test comes when Nvidia’s employees, customers and partners, and, indirectly, the millions of Americans with Nvidia in their 401(k) plans, have to decide whether an AI economy built largely on the judgment of Huang still makes sense. The romantic interest is Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy who was feeding information back to Beijing. In short, the stakes reach well beyond Nvidia, given how many tech and financial partners depend on its place at the center of the AI economy. “I’m responsible for an entire industry ,” Huang recently told Bloomberg in a sit-down.

A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations in late October as “ groundless smears and slanders ,” and no one has been charged. But U.S. intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Donald Trump about their concerns a year ago, and unnamed senior officials inside the Trump administration told the Times that they doubt Huang could have remained unaware all that time of Alice Huang’s intelligence-gathering role for China. When Trump was first briefed, the Times reported, officials didn’t believe Huang knew, and it isn’t clear whether their assessment has changed. The board, meanwhile, says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised.

The question is whether Huang can survive this. To think through what could come next, this editor spoke Sunday with famed professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which has hosted Huang at its CEO summits. Sonnenfeld likes Huang, he said, and he called Huang’s career salvageable but put the odds at “about a 50-50.” He also had a lot more food for thought.

First, the damage. Until now, Huang has been “revered and trusted by everybody in technology,” Sonnenfeld noted. But he called this episode “remarkably poor judgment.” Even if Huang was merely naive, he said, “any employee in Nvidia other than him would be fired over this,” and the recklessness alone would mean “an irretrievable loss of confidence.”

Sonnenfeld suggested that Huang’s saving grace could be what social psychologists call idiosyncrasy credits , if he can prove he was being duped. The term comes from Edwin Hollander, a social psychologist who proposed in a 1958 paper that people earn latitude in a group by showing competence and following its rules. Huang has been earning latitude since he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. But all that goodwill can run out when a screw-up looks self-serving or touches the group’s core norms. Here that group includes Nvidia’s board, its roughly 42,000 employees who are bound by security rules, and, in a looser sense, the U.S. government, given it restricts its exports.

We also talked about precedents, except, as it turns out, there really are none for what’s unfolding right now. Executives who survive personal scandals sometimes pick up where they left off at another company, Sonnenfeld observed. Former HP CEO Mark Hurd is one example. Between 2005 and 2010, he drove HP to the top of the tech industry by revenue, then was pressured to resign after he filed inaccurate expense reports that hid a personal relationship with a contractor. Oracle hired him about a month later. Huang has no equivalent because Nvidia is his company

As for the bench at Nvidia, that doesn’t really exist either. While there is typically a hierarchy inside companies of Nvidia’s scale and importance, Huang has kept things as flat as possible, with about 60 direct reports by his own account. That structure makes it hard to figure out who would succeed him (though his children, both of whom work at Nvidia, are sometimes the subject of succession speculation ). That won’t stop the worldwide guessing game that’s sure to follow. And boards in crisis often reach for a “messianic solution” from outside, Sonnenfeld said, floating former Google CEO Eric Schmidt as one idea.

Nvidia’s role at the center of a massive and complex circular financing web is what makes this particular predicament so tricky and, undoubtedly, terrifying for a wide number of constituents. Nvidia isn’t just the biggest provider of chips driving the AI boom but also largely the bank behind the buildout. In addition to stakes in hundreds of smaller startups, Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave and Nebius. In August, it also signed preliminary agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion over time, and Huang has said Nvidia could backstop up to a quarter of it. The move was widely interpreted as a way to spread risk. Still, a leadership crisis at the center is how a stumble becomes a collapse.

So what’s Nvidia’s board likely doing right now? Sonnenfeld noted that Huang’s constant, public advocacy for selling advanced chips to China had already made people anxious. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, whose company Nvidia has backed, had a lot to say about selling chips to China at Davos back in January, likening it to “ selling nuclear weapons to North Korea .”

Now the board’s independent members — meaning everyone but Huang — will have to establish what technology reached China if any, and by what routes, including by better understanding Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed. The Singapore cloud company, which grew out of a Chinese gaming business and became Nvidia’s largest buyer in Southeast Asia, bought roughly $2 billion of its chips , the New York Times reported in October 2025, raising broader questions about whether it was helping China circumvent U.S. export restrictions by re-exporting the chips to China or renting them to Chinese customers remotely. (An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill after the Times report that the allegations were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year .”)

In the meantime, Huang will keep running the company, Nvidia said Sunday. That’ll be a tall order, even for a CEO who already spends much of his time traveling the world to promote Nvidia. For starters, three House chairmen want a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18. Nvidia is also reporting its newest earnings on November 17. Sonnenfeld expects that even if Huang keeps the title, he’ll have to hand off some of the day-to-day decision-making.

Only one thing is certain right now. Huang doesn’t own the kind of super-voting stock that would cement his power at Nvidia. Sonnenfeld often argues for dual-class structures that empower founders, and he says Huang’s success without one has been the best counterargument to that case. But if Huang had one, Sonnenfeld continued, removing him would be harder.

This episode may be remembered as a pivotal moment for how the tech industry guards its secrets. Sonnenfeld argues tech has been “way too lax” compared with defense contractors that face clearance regimes. The arrest last month of an OpenAI engineer points to the same problem. He was accused of hiding a recording device behind a TV in an executive conference room, and while OpenAI has said it has no indication that model weights, source code, or customer data were accessed, the case highlights how exposed tech companies are to people who get close.

Huang may well survive the investigation (Sonnenfeld hopes the board clears him of knowingly aiding anyone). The bigger test comes when Nvidia’s employees, customers and partners, and, indirectly, the millions of Americans with Nvidia in their 401(k) plans, have to decide whether an AI economy built largely on the judgment of Huang still makes sense.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang's three-decade reign atop Nvidia hangs in the balance as the chipmaker's board investigates the CEO's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Yale leadership expert Jeffrey Sonnenfeld puts Huang's survival odds at roughly 50-50, marking the most serious threat yet to the architect of the AI boom. The probe follows revelations that China's Ministry of State Security targeted Huang through a tech executive with close personal ties. Nvidia's board has launched an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang over his relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, plunging the world's most valuable chipmaker into a leadership crisis that could reshape the AI industry. Yale School of Management's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, who advises boards on CEO succession, told TechCrunch he estimates it's "about a 50-50" chance Huang remains in his role. The investigation follows a bombshell US intelligence memo revealing that China's Ministry of State Security recruited a tech executive to cultivate a relationship with Huang and gather intelligence on the CEO who controls the chips powering the global AI race. The suspected operative maintained what sources described as a close personal relationship with Huang, raising questions about potential security breaches at a company whose technology the US government considers critical to national security. Huang has led Nvidia since co-founding the company in 1993, steering it from a graphics card maker into a $3 trillion colossus that supplies the GPUs behind ChatGPT, Claude, and virtually every major AI system. His signature leather jacket and technical evangelism made him the face of the AI revolution, but that 33-year tenure now faces its gravest test. Sonnenfeld's 50-50 assessment carries weight. He runs Yale's Chief Executive Leadership Institute and has counseled boards through crises at companies from Boeing to Wells Fargo. The company controls roughly 80% of the AI accelerator market, with customers including OpenAI, Meta, Google, and Microsoft all dependent on its H100 and H200 chips. Just days before the investigation became public, Nvidia announced partnerships with Samsung and Korean firms on factory-floor AI deployments and opened its NVLink platform to Korean companies building sovereign AI infrastructure. The Chinese espionage angle adds another layer of complexity to Nvidia's already fraught relationship with Beijing. US export controls have banned the company from selling its most advanced chips to China, yet investigations found Nvidia's H200 chips reached Chinese buyers through a ghost company the Commerce Department had approved despite the firm operating from empty offices. The board now must weigh whether Huang's relationship with the suspected operative compromised the company's compliance with those restrictions or exposed sensitive technology. Industry insiders say the board faces an impossible calculus. He personally designed the company's strategy of betting on parallel processing years before AI made GPUs indispensable. He negotiated the deals that made Nvidia the sole supplier to virtually every AI lab. Analysts estimate his leadership added over $2 trillion to the company's market capitalization in the past two years alone. But the national security implications of a CEO potentially compromised by Chinese intelligence could force the board's hand regardless of Huang's value. The investigation comes as cybersecurity experts warn AI is ushering in a "dark age" for digital defenses, with AI-powered attacks overwhelming traditional security measures. The suspected espionage operation against Huang represents exactly the kind of sophisticated influence campaign that blends personal relationships with intelligence gathering, making it difficult to detect and even harder to defend against. Nvidia hasn't publicly commented on the investigation's timeline or scope. The company's board includes former executives from Google, Cisco, and the semiconductor industry, giving it deep technical expertise but also close ties to the same tech ecosystem that depends on Nvidia's continued stability. If the board determines Huang must step aside, the company has no obvious successor. Unlike Apple, which has groomed internal candidates for years, Nvidia's leadership structure revolves entirely around its founder. Investors are watching for any sign of how the investigation might resolve. Nvidia's stock has become a proxy for AI sentiment across the market, with its quarterly earnings moving the entire tech sector. A forced CEO transition would trigger questions about deal continuity, product roadmap execution, and whether Nvidia can maintain its technological edge without the visionary who created it. The 50-50 odds Sonnenfeld cited suggest even experts can't predict which way the board will break. The investigation into Jensen Huang represents more than a corporate governance crisis - it's a potential inflection point for the entire AI industry. If Nvidia's board decides the national security risks outweigh Huang's irreplaceable expertise, the company that makes AI possible will have to reinvent itself without the founder who built it. The next few weeks will determine whether the AI boom continues under Huang's leadership or enters a new, uncertain chapter.

passages: Nvidia has announced that it is opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who was reportedly recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on the company.
President Trump has loosened those restrictions but still bars sales of Nvidia’s most powerful chips to Chinese firms, and the Commerce Department must approve individual firms to handle the chips.
Just as importantly, Jensen Huang has gotten quite cozy with Donald Trump, and there is concern about what insights into the administration’s deliberations around AI he may have been privy to.

A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. > The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.
While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.

A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. > The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders. While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. > The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate. The New York Times reported last month that Huang had developed a “close relationship” with the Megaspeed executive, which he later admitted was romantic in nature in a memo to the company. Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia and is the subject of a Commerce Department investigation into whether it was smuggling AI chips to China. The company’s AI chips are viewed as crucial to the US maintaining technological supremacy. President Trump has loosened those restrictions but still bars sales of Nvidia’s most powerful chips to Chinese firms, and the Commerce Department must approve individual firms to handle the chips. Just as importantly, Jensen Huang has gotten quite cozy with Donald Trump, and there is concern about what insights into the administration’s deliberations around AI he may have been privy to. And whether any of that information may have been shared with Alice Huang, and eventually found its way to Beijing.

Beijing pushed back on NVIDIA's story quickly. Bloomberg reported that China's Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun called the spy allegation "unsubstantiated" and "nothing but smears against China." Reuters reported that a planned Korea event involving Madison Huang, a senior director at NVIDIA, was canceled due to "unavoidable internal circumstances at Nvidia," while NVIDIA AI Day Seoul is proceeding.

Some analysts see a near-term concern on NVIDIA and the risk that Huang could ultimately lose the CEO title. The company's deal flow continues, though. On November 9, NVIDIA announced a partnership with SK Telecom and Korean chip startup Rebellions on sovereign artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure built on NVLink Fusion.

The geopolitical stakes for NVIDIA are rising too, since Bloomberg reported the episode could complicate the meeting between Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen next week. Chip stocks are also coming off a broader post-midterm sell-off, and NVIDIA stock is down 26% over the past month.

AMD was extending its gains from the prior session as money rotated away from NVIDIA's company-specific risk. The chipmaker also had news of its own on November 9, saying its 5th Gen EPYC server processors power the host infrastructure for Alphabet unit Google Cloud's newest Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) system, the first cloud TPU system with hardware-enforced confidential computing. According to AMD, EPYC is the host central processing unit (CPU) of choice across more than 10 leading hyperscalers and frontier AI labs, including systems built with NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs) and custom accelerators.

Steadiness at Intel suggests the selling remains contained to NVIDIA. Broadcom ( NASDAQ:AVGO ) stock is at $302.58, up 3%. Meanwhile, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( NYSE:TSM ) stock is at $382, up 2%, adding further evidence that the sell-off is NVIDIA-specific.

NVIDIA sells an integrated platform that pairs its GPUs with networking, full systems and its CUDA software ecosystem, which keeps customers tied to its hardware. AMD is a diverse challenger, selling Instinct AI accelerators and EPYC server CPUs while outsourcing manufacturing to third-party foundries. Intel both designs and manufactures chips, and it's rebuilding around Xeon data-center processors and Intel Foundry.

Those differences matter when leadership comes into question. NVIDIA's platform story is closely tied to its co-founder's vision, so doubts about Huang's future hit the stock directly. Intel's management, by contrast, expects the personal computer (PC) slowdown to persist through at least the first half of 2027, a separate concern from leadership.

NVIDIA's upcoming earnings report is reportedly scheduled for November 17, a date the company hasn't confirmed. Shareholders may press management on the board review and Huang's role then. NVIDIA's guidance for Q3 FY2027 called for revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%.

Demand is a clear positive, with Huang stating on the August 26 earnings call that "Our entire supply chain is challenged, and everybody is really running flat out." That expansion still has to be powered and cooled by somebody, and we featured seven non-chipmaker suppliers riding the same wave in a free report. On the bearish side sit key-person risk, China tensions ahead of the APEC meeting and the chance that NVIDIA's review drags on. It may make sense to stay cautious until the board's review of Huang settles.

On Sunday, Nvidia’s Board of Directors announced an independent investigation into founder and CEO Jensen Huang. The inquiry follows multiple intelligence and media reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort involving a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy — along with the admission of an affair.

The investigation occurs against the backdrop of a severe tech stock sell-off, with nearly $2 trillion erased because of fears of an AI bubble. Nvidia, which has served as the cornerstone of this gold rush, dropped 4% in overnight trading value, as it’s now under a microscope of geopolitical and governance concerns.
Here is the timeline of events leading up to the board’s investigation.
Before we get into the market fallout, let’s run through the timeline of what happened.
And that brings you up to what happened yesterday.
Jensen Huang’s internal email to Nvidia employees has now been leaked. In it, he wrote: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.”
Shortly after, Nvidia’s Board of Directors officially announced an independent investigation into the matter, overseen by outside counsel.

The board states it “prioritizes U.S. national and economic security,” and while it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, it will examine all available information. The board also notes that Huang is fully cooperating with the review.

Lawmakers have already expressed alarm over the national security implications of the relationship, as members of the House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence Committees already requested Huang provide a closed-door briefing . The ball was already rolling on this part.

Meanwhile, speaking to reporters last night, President Trump downplayed the severity of the allegations against his AI adviser. Trump states, “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it,” adding that he still intends to bring Huang along on an upcoming trip to Asia.

extraction.body: A US memo alleges Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive US intelligence believes was recruited as a Chinese spy. Republican lawmakers now want Huang to testify. Read the full story here. The US government, as per a report, believes Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese woman recruited to spy for China's main intelligence agency. According to a Financial Times report citing people familiar with the matter, US officials in a memo shared earlier this year noted that information obtained by American intelligence agencies suggests that the Nvidia CEO was an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of the US chip group. The US intelligence community believes Alice Huang was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security. As per the report, the memo was shared with a small group of top US government officials shortly before President Donald Trump travelled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping. The White House and CIA declined to comment. Also read | China hired businesswoman to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang: Report Photographs and videos showing Huang with the Megaspeed executive are being widely circulated on social media. In June 2024, just weeks before Megaspeed began its purchases, photos posted to LinkedIn showed Jensen Huang alongside Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei following a local technology trade show, where they drank whiskey with other AI executives. A year later, in May 2025, they were seen together again, leaving a restaurant in Taipei after a business dinner with other AI suppliers. She waited behind Jensen Huang as he spoke to Taiwanese journalists outside the restaurant. It is not clear when the two first met. However, Alice Huang had posted photos of herself with him on her social media feed. Following the intelligence allegations, her personal social media feeds, where she had posted the June 2024 bar photos and the May 2025 restaurant photos, were scrubbed, hidden or deactivated. Nvidia has declined to comment on the government memo and the assertions that its chief executive had an intimate relationship with Alice Huang. The company has previously said he meets "thousands of customer executives every year". Megaspeed, which was spun off from a Chinese gaming company in 2023, has come under US scrutiny for allegedly smuggling advanced Nvidia chips into China in violation of US export controls. Nvidia had previously launched an internal probe into the allegations but found that there was no evidence of wrongdoing. Also read | Midterm loss forces Trump White House to post AI-generated reminder: 'Still your president' | WATCH The revelation about the memo comes a day after top Republican lawmakers asked the Nvidia CEO to appear in private before the House China, foreign affairs and intelligence committees to answer questions about a New York Times report that US intelligence had concluded he was the target of a Chinese spying operation. They also wanted to ask Huang about the security protocols the company has in place. The US government has been investigating companies, particularly in south-east Asia, believed to be smuggling advanced chips into China. The focus has intensified as competition between the US and China in AI has grown sharper, with Washington increasingly concerned about Beijing's ability to obtain chips that would accelerate its military modernisation. US national security officials reportedly have also privately expressed frustration about Huang, who personally lobbied Trump earlier this year to allow Nvidia to export the H200 chip to customers in China. Notably, Huang has held multiple meetings with Trump since the president began his second term in 2025. When Trump flew to China in May for the summit with Xi, Huang was not among the chief executives who departed Washington on Air Force One. After Trump learnt he was not included in the group, he called the Nvidia CEO, who flew to Alaska and boarded the presidential jet during a stopover. In September, Huang also attended the state dinner Trump held for Xi during his US visit. extraction.body: Three House Republican committee leaders asked Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to sit for a closed-door briefing on his relationship with a tech executive reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang unveiled Thursday, using the acronym for the People's Republic of China. They are seeking information on Huang's interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage," they wrote in the brief message, which is dated Wednesday. The letter does not specify which reports it is referring to. But The New York Times reported last week that U.S. intelligence found Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen determined to be funneling information to Beijing, had "developed a close relationship" with Jensen Huang. President Donald Trump , who himself has forged close ties with Jensen Huang as he champions the U.S. artificial intelligence industry, was briefed about a year ago on those intelligence findings, the Times reported. Trump "chose not to do anything with the information," according to the newspaper, which cited interviews with people briefed on the surveillance and other sources. The letter to Huang was signed by House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark. Nvidia did not directly respond when asked by CNBC to comment on the letter and confirm whether Huang would attend the lawmakers' proposed briefing. Nvidia instead provided a statement that largely mirrored the one it previously sent the Times, in which a spokesperson suggested Jensen Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were no different from his meetings with other executive clients. "Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security," the spokesperson said in the statement. "Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," the spokesperson said. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know." A spokeswoman for Mast did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for additional information. Megaspeed did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment. The lawmakers invited the Nvidia CEO to appear for an in-person joint briefing on Nov. 18. Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17. "China's access to that sensitive U.S. tech is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the committee leaders wrote. Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
The chairs of the House committees on China, foreign affairs, and intelligence wrote to Huang this week asking him to appear before a joint closed-door briefing for their committees on November 18.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the People’s Republic of China’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford wrote.

“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.

The New York Times last week wrote that US intelligence officials believed Huang had been the target of a Chinese spy operation. The concerns center on a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company that has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia’s chips.

Nvidia has rejected the claims and on Thursday would not say if Huang would appear before Congress. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job. Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.
“Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information—not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security,” it added.

The lawmakers said they wanted Huang to discuss the security protocols Nvidia had in place to protect against “foreign adversary espionage.” The company said its chief executive had an “outstanding security team” that travels with him.
The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity.

Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.
The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed.

Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter.

The company’s supply chain has come under increasing scrutiny as US export controls have prompted increased smuggling of its chips. Earlier this year Wally Liaw, a co-founder of Supermicro, one of Nvidia’s key supply chain partners, was arrested in the US and charged with smuggling Nvidia chips into China. He denies any wrongdoing and has pleaded not guilty.

They emphasized, "It is crucial for Congress to understand the extent to which U.S. national security has been exposed to risk." This request indicates growing congressional pressure surrounding the investigation into the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who is suspected of Chinese espionage. Alice Huang is a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-headquartered data center company. She was photographed drinking alongside Jensen Huang and other artificial intelligence (AI) company executives at a bar in Taiwan in June 2024, and was spotted with him again in May of last year. Alice Huang herself reportedly flaunted her ties by posting photos with Jensen Huang on social media, which she allegedly used to raise investment funds. Previously, The New York Times (NYT) reported that Alice Huang is suspected of maintaining a close relationship with Jensen Huang and leaking information to China. The NYT also reported that President Donald Trump was briefed on the matter by intelligence agencies but took no action. The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that authorities in at least three countries are concerned that Alice Huang may have leaked sensitive information regarding Nvidia chips to the Chinese government. coreStoryFacts.text: Three House Republican committee leaders asked Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to sit for a closed-door briefing on his relationship with a tech executive reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.

They are seeking information on Huang's interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage," they wrote in the brief message, which is dated Wednesday.
Nvidia did not directly respond when asked by CNBC to comment on the letter and confirm whether Huang would attend the lawmakers' proposed briefing.
The letter does not specify which reports it is referring to.
Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings on Nov.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang unveiled Thursday, using the acronym for the People's Republic of China.
"Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security," the spokesperson said in the statement.

President Donald Trump , who himself has forged close ties with Jensen Huang as he champions the U.S. artificial intelligence industry, was briefed about a year ago on those intelligence findings, the Times reported.
A spokeswoman for Mast did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for additional information.

Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.
Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.
Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.
“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.
It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.
The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed.
The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity.

Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.

Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter.

They are seeking information on Huang's interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage," they wrote in the brief message, which is dated Wednesday. The letter does not specify which reports it is referring to. But The New York Times reported last week that U.S. intelligence found Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen determined to be funneling information to Beijing, had "developed a close relationship" with Jensen Huang. President Donald Trump , who himself has forged close ties with Jensen Huang as he champions the U.S. artificial intelligence industry, was briefed about a year ago on those intelligence findings, the Times reported. Trump "chose not to do anything with the information," according to the newspaper, which cited interviews with people briefed on the surveillance and other sources. The letter to Huang was signed by House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark. Nvidia did not directly respond when asked by CNBC to comment on the letter and confirm whether Huang would attend the lawmakers' proposed briefing. Nvidia instead provided a statement that largely mirrored the one it previously sent the Times, in which a spokesperson suggested Jensen Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were no different from his meetings with other executive clients. "Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security," the spokesperson said in the statement. "Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," the spokesperson said. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know." A spokeswoman for Mast did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for additional information. Megaspeed did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment. The lawmakers invited the Nvidia CEO to appear for an in-person joint briefing on Nov. 18. Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17. "China's access to that sensitive U.S. tech is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the committee leaders wrote. passages: Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.

Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
The chairs of the House committees on China, foreign affairs, and intelligence wrote to Huang this week asking him to appear before a joint closed-door briefing for their committees on November 18.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the People’s Republic of China’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford wrote.

“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.

The New York Times last week wrote that US intelligence officials believed Huang had been the target of a Chinese spy operation. The concerns center on a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company that has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia’s chips.

Nvidia has rejected the claims and on Thursday would not say if Huang would appear before Congress. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job. Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.
“Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information—not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security,” it added.

The lawmakers said they wanted Huang to discuss the security protocols Nvidia had in place to protect against “foreign adversary espionage.” The company said its chief executive had an “outstanding security team” that travels with him.
The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity.

Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.
The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed.

Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter.

The company’s supply chain has come under increasing scrutiny as US export controls have prompted increased smuggling of its chips. Earlier this year Wally Liaw, a co-founder of Supermicro, one of Nvidia’s key supply chain partners, was arrested in the US and charged with smuggling Nvidia chips into China. He denies any wrongdoing and has pleaded not guilty.

NetThunder, a company that posted this photo on social media, introduced Alice Huang as "Megaspeed Chairperson Alice Wong." The U.S. Congress has summoned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to directly explain his relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. According to Axios on the 5th (local time), Representative Brian Mast, Republican Chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Representative John Moolenaar, Chairman of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and Representative Rick Crawford, member of the Intelligence Committee, sent a letter to Jensen Huang that day, requesting his attendance at a joint, closed-door briefing by the three committees. In the letter, they asked Huang to explain Nvidia's security systems designed to protect the company from foreign adversaries, as well as his interactions with Alice Huang. They stated, "Recent reports raise serious national security concerns regarding the possibility of China accessing sensitive U.S. technologies and information," adding, "The issues of Chinese infiltration and access to advanced U.S. technology are core investigative matters for the three committees during this session." They emphasized, "It is crucial for Congress to understand the extent to which U.S. national security has been exposed to risk." This request indicates growing congressional pressure surrounding the investigation into the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who is suspected of Chinese espionage. Alice Huang is a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-headquartered data center company. She was photographed drinking alongside Jensen Huang and other artificial intelligence (AI) company executives at a bar in Taiwan in June 2024, and was spotted with him again in May of last year. Alice Huang herself reportedly flaunted her ties by posting photos with Jensen Huang on social media, which she allegedly used to raise investment funds. Previously, The New York Times (NYT) reported that Alice Huang is suspected of maintaining a close relationship with Jensen Huang and leaking information to China. The NYT also reported that President Donald Trump was briefed on the matter by intelligence agencies but took no action. The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that authorities in at least three countries are concerned that Alice Huang may have leaked sensitive information regarding Nvidia chips to the Chinese government. However, Nvidia has denied the allegations, stating that Jensen Huang's contact with Alice Huang was merely routine business interaction and that no national security-related information was leaked. Nvidia has not released a statement regarding the House's summons. The Chinese government previously dismissed allegations of Chinese espionage targeting Nvidia as "groundless speculation." (Photo: Capture of a NetThunder LinkedIn post, Yonhap News) ※ Please note: This article was translated by AI and may contain errors.

sources.title: Strategy and Riot Fall 4%, Cipher Digital Declines 3% as MSCI Index Rules and Convertible Sale Weigh - AOL.com
passages: An index decision and a fresh debt sale are pulling two crypto-linked names lower.
Strategy ( NASDAQ:MSTR ) stock is down 4% to $145.50 during the morning session after an index rule change from MSCI ( NYSE:MSCI ).
Strategy (MSTR) faces MSCI index exclusion risk at the November review, while Cipher Digital (CIFR) drops 3% after pricing zero-coupon convertible notes for Barber Lake.

As a Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) miner, Riot runs a different model from both, since Strategy holds the token as its main treasury asset and Cipher Digital is converting former Bitcoin mining sites into AI data centers.
MSCI announced revised index eligibility rules for non-operating companies, replacing interim limits on companies with large digital asset reserves with financial tests.
Those tests take effect with MSCI's November index review, and Strategy is among the companies MSCI previously identified as potentially ineligible.
ETFs tied to MSCI equity indexes held a record $2.818 trillion at the end of Q2 2026.
As the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, Strategy reported 846,000 bitcoin on its books as of Q2, plus $6.7 billion in convertible debt.
Strategy shares are falling even with Bitcoin at $81,903 and higher over the past 24 hours, a split that puts the index question at the center of the selloff.
That pressure leaves Strategy stock down 5% year to date (YTD).
For Cipher Digital, the open variable is execution on the data center projects its new notes fund.
Investors should consider keeping their position sizes modest until MSCI's decision on Strategy settles.
A stronger Bitcoin price may not offset index-driven selling in Strategy shares if MSCI moves to exclude the company.
CleanSpark (CLSK) signed a $6.6 billion, 20-year lease as WGMI slides 2%, weighed down by Cipher Digital's dominant 18% fund position.
The upside for Strategy rests on MSCI's rule that current index members are removed only after failing its screen in two consecutive annual filing periods.
