extraction.body: The US and Ukraine say they have created an "updated and refined" plan to end the war with Russia, seemingly modifying a Trump-backed plan Kyiv saw as too sympathetic to Moscow. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is leading the talks, says discussions on the new peace plan are perhaps "the best … so far" since Russia's invasion. Negotiations between Ukraine and the US are continuing, despite the White House previously saying Ukraine had until Thursday to accept its initial peace proposal or the US would withdraw support. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says ongoing discussions with Ukrainian negotiators in Geneva have been "probably the best … so far" in terms of progressing a potential peace deal between Russia and Ukraine. The US and Ukraine on Sunday issued a joint statement saying they had created an "updated and refined peace framework" to end the war with Russia, apparently modifying a plan drafted by the Trump administration that Kyiv and its allies saw as too sympathetic to Moscow. While the joint statement did not provide specifics, a separate release from the White House said the new version of the proposal included strengthened security guarantees, and that the Ukrainian delegation had said it "reflects their national interests". Ukrainian negotiator Andriy Yermak speaks alongside Mr Rubio in Geneva on Sunday. ( Keystone via AP Photo: Martial Trezzini ) The negotiators' optimistic tone was in stark contrast to a social media post by US President Donald Trump earlier that morning, in which he criticised Ukraine's leaders and accused them of being ungrateful for American support during Russia's invasion. Mr Trump also hit out at European nations for continuing to buy Russian oil. "UKRAINE 'LEADERSHIP' HAS EXPRESSED ZERO GRATITUDE FOR OUR EFFORTS, AND EUROPE CONTINUES TO BUY OIL FROM RUSSIA," Mr Trump posted on his Truth Social platform. In a sombre address to Ukraine's citizens, the president vowed he would not betray Ukrainian interests in the US-led peace process. Mr Trump also lamented the "human catastrophe" of the war, but did not directly criticise Moscow for its role. "I INHERITED A WAR THAT SHOULD HAVE NEVER HAPPENED, A WAR THAT IS A LOSER FOR EVERYONE, ESPECIALLY THE MILLIONS OF PEOPLE THAT HAVE SO NEEDLESSLY DIED," he wrote. In a response on X ahead of the talks, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said blame for the conflict should be directed entirely at Russia and its president, Vladimir Putin. He also sought to reassure the US president he was thankful for American support. "Ukraine is grateful to the United States, to every American heart, and personally to President Trump for the assistance that — starting with the Javelins — has been saving Ukrainian lives," he wrote. Mr Trump's post came shortly before Mr Rubio and special envoy Steve Witkoff met with European leaders in Geneva on Sunday to discuss a 28-point peace plan released by the White House on Friday. The plan calls for Ukraine to cede territory it currently controls, accept limits on its military and renounce ambitions to join NATO, echoing many demands Russia has made in recent years. Mr Zelenskyy has criticised the plan, saying his country faces the choice of either losing its dignity or losing the backing of a key ally , given the Trump administration is threatening to withdraw support if Kyiv does not accept the plan by Thursday. Donald Trump welcomed Volodymyr Zelenskyy to the White House in October this year. ( Reuters: Nathan Howard ) The plan was also lambasted by a bipartisan group of senators critical of the White House's approach to the Ukraine conflict, who told a security conference in Canada on Saturday that Mr Rubio had personally told them it amounted to a "wish list of the Russians". European leaders say they were not consulted on the plan, and Republican senator Mike Rounds even suggested the White House was "not responsible" for the proposal's text, adding it "looked more like it was written in Russian to begin with". "It is based on input from the Russian side. But it is also based on previous and ongoing input from Ukraine," he wrote. The spat threatened to undercut Mr Rubio's messaging as he sought to reach a deal with Ukraine's delegation to the talks in Geneva on Sunday. Speaking to reporters midway through the meeting, Mr Rubio said the talks had been "probably [the] best meeting and day we've had so far in this entire process". He later said changes would be made to the plan to work towards a solution that both Ukraine and the US could support. "Obviously, this will ultimately have to be signed off with our presidents, although I feel very comfortable about that happening given the progress we've made," Mr Rubio said. "We are much further ahead than when we began this morning." European leaders, for their part, have voiced alarm at the Trump administration's plan . An alternative peace plan put forward by the UK, France and Germany at the summit pushed back on proposed limits to Kyiv's armed forces and territorial concessions, according to a document seen by Reuters. The document proposes that Ukraine's military be capped at 800,000 "in peacetime" rather than a blanket cap of 600,000 proposed by the US plan. It proposes that Ukraine receive a security guarantee from the United States similar to NATO's Article 5 clause. And it further suggests "negotiations on territorial swaps will start from the Line of Contact" between Ukrainian and Russian forces, rather than pre-determining that certain areas should be recognised as "de facto Russian", as the US plan suggests. Speaking after several rounds of talks between Ukraine and the US, Ukrainian negotiator Rustem Umerov said the latest version of the US draft plan for ending the war in Ukraine now included most of Kyiv's "key priorities". "The current version of the document, although still in the final stages of approval, already reflects most of Ukraine's key priorities," he said. "We look forward to further progress throughout the day."

The US and Ukraine on Sunday issued a joint statement saying they had created an "updated and refined peace framework" to end the war with Russia, apparently modifying a plan drafted by the Trump administration that Kyiv and its allies saw as too sympathetic to Moscow. While the joint statement did not provide specifics, a separate release from the White House said the new version of the proposal included strengthened security guarantees, and that the Ukrainian delegation had said it "reflects their national interests". Ukrainian negotiator Andriy Yermak speaks alongside Mr Rubio in Geneva on Sunday. ( Keystone via AP Photo: Martial Trezzini ) The negotiators' optimistic tone was in stark contrast to a social media post by US President Donald Trump earlier that morning, in which he criticised Ukraine's leaders and accused them of being ungrateful for American support during Russia's invasion. Mr Trump also hit out at European nations for continuing to buy Russian oil. "UKRAINE 'LEADERSHIP' HAS EXPRESSED ZERO GRATITUDE FOR OUR EFFORTS, AND EUROPE CONTINUES TO BUY OIL FROM RUSSIA," Mr Trump posted on his Truth Social platform. In a sombre address to Ukraine's citizens, the president vowed he would not betray Ukrainian interests in the US-led peace process. Mr Trump also lamented the "human catastrophe" of the war, but did not directly criticise Moscow for its role. "I INHERITED A WAR THAT SHOULD HAVE NEVER HAPPENED, A WAR THAT IS A LOSER FOR EVERYONE, ESPECIALLY THE MILLIONS OF PEOPLE THAT HAVE SO NEEDLESSLY DIED," he wrote. In a response on X ahead of the talks, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said blame for the conflict should be directed entirely at Russia and its president, Vladimir Putin. He also sought to reassure the US president he was thankful for American support. "Ukraine is grateful to the United States, to every American heart, and personally to President Trump for the assistance that — starting with the Javelins — has been saving Ukrainian lives," he wrote. Mr Trump's post came shortly before Mr Rubio and special envoy Steve Witkoff met with European leaders in Geneva on Sunday to discuss a 28-point peace plan released by the White House on Friday. The plan calls for Ukraine to cede territory it currently controls, accept limits on its military and renounce ambitions to join NATO, echoing many demands Russia has made in recent years. Mr Zelenskyy has criticised the plan, saying his country faces the choice of either losing its dignity or losing the backing of a key ally , given the Trump administration is threatening to withdraw support if Kyiv does not accept the plan by Thursday. Donald Trump welcomed Volodymyr Zelenskyy to the White House in October this year. ( Reuters: Nathan Howard ) The plan was also lambasted by a bipartisan group of senators critical of the White House's approach to the Ukraine conflict, who told a security conference in Canada on Saturday that Mr Rubio had personally told them it amounted to a "wish list of the Russians". European leaders say they were not consulted on the plan, and Republican senator Mike Rounds even suggested the White House was "not responsible" for the proposal's text, adding it "looked more like it was written in Russian to begin with". "It is based on input from the Russian side. But it is also based on previous and ongoing input from Ukraine," he wrote. The spat threatened to undercut Mr Rubio's messaging as he sought to reach a deal with Ukraine's delegation to the talks in Geneva on Sunday. Speaking to reporters midway through the meeting, Mr Rubio said the talks had been "probably [the] best meeting and day we've had so far in this entire process". He later said changes would be made to the plan to work towards a solution that both Ukraine and the US could support. "Obviously, this will ultimately have to be signed off with our presidents, although I feel very comfortable about that happening given the progress we've made," Mr Rubio said. "We are much further ahead than when we began this morning." European leaders, for their part, have voiced alarm at the Trump administration's plan . An alternative peace plan put forward by the UK, France and Germany at the summit pushed back on proposed limits to Kyiv's armed forces and territorial concessions, according to a document seen by Reuters. The document proposes that Ukraine's military be capped at 800,000 "in peacetime" rather than a blanket cap of 600,000 proposed by the US plan. It proposes that Ukraine receive a security guarantee from the United States similar to NATO's Article 5 clause. And it further suggests "negotiations on territorial swaps will start from the Line of Contact" between Ukrainian and Russian forces, rather than pre-determining that certain areas should be recognised as "de facto Russian", as the US plan suggests. Speaking after several rounds of talks between Ukraine and the US, Ukrainian negotiator Rustem Umerov said the latest version of the US draft plan for ending the war in Ukraine now included most of Kyiv's "key priorities". "The current version of the document, although still in the final stages of approval, already reflects most of Ukraine's key priorities," he said. "We look forward to further progress throughout the day."

extraction.body: European leaders' commitment to security guarantees for Ukraine is important but not crucial, say experts. What about the US and Russia? One of the main topics of discussion in Berlin on December 14 and 15 was the post-ceasefire security guarantees that Ukraine would receive in the event of an agreement with Russia . In addition to European leaders, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, US special envoy Steve Witkoff, and Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump took part in the talks. Afterwards, there was a telephone call with the US president. At a joint press conference, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Zelenskyy were upbeat about the progress made. They said that there had been discussion of security guarantees akin to those offered by Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty and territorial questions. In their "Leader's statement on Ukraine," European leaders referred to a "European-led 'multinational force Ukraine' made up from contributions from willing nations." This would "assist in the regeneration of Ukraine's forces, in securing Ukraine's skies, and in supporting safer seas, including through operating inside Ukraine." The statement also outlined commitments in the event of peace to a " US led ceasefire monitoring and verification mechanism with international participation," as well as "a legally binding commitment, subject to national procedures, to take measures to restore peace and security in the case of a future armed attack" on Ukraine . Citing its own sources, the Reuters news agency reported that Zelenskyy had agreed during the talks in Berlin to drop Ukraine's NATO bid in return for security guarantees from the West. It remains unclear what the guarantees for Ukraine could look like in concrete terms. "These measures may include armed force, intelligence and logistical assistance, economic and diplomatic actions," the European leaders' statement said. So far, the US has not issued an official statement. According to the AFP news agency, a US official said that the "basis of the agreement is basically to have really, really strong guarantees — Article Five like — also a very, very strong deterrence." This reportedly did not involve the deployment of US troops. Susan Stewart from the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) told DW that the European leader statement and the fact that it outlined concrete measures was "very important" for Ukraine. She said that the potential security guarantees were similar to those granted to NATO members by Article 5 , which obliges the alliance to support a member state if it is attacked. "Article 5 of the NATO treaty does not stipulate that an attack must be responded to with military means, but rather that each state should must use the means it deems necessary and appropriate," she pointed out. Stewart said it would only be possibly to assess the guarantees thoroughly once all the details had been published. "But I think it's very important that this step has now been taken, to list these points and say: 'Yes, we as Europeans are ready to do this.'" She said that the statement indicated that "certain agreements with the US" had already been made. In the opinion of Claudia Major, a security expert at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, the security guarantees for Ukraine are not comparable to those granted NATO members. "It is support. However, it is not a legally binding obligation to defend Ukraine in the event of a new attack," she told German public broadcaster ARD. She said that on the basis of what is currently known there was no way of deducing what might happen concretely in the wake of a future Russian attack. "Will troops be sent? Will someone come to defend Ukraine, as would happen in NATO? This is not the case." He did not think that Russia would make concessions since it believes it is "on the path to victory," he said. "The specific issue here is Donbass, whether or not the Russians can effectively take possession of the entire region. At the moment, the Russians are insisting on this. Until this happens, Putin will continue this war. Reisner was also skeptical about the potential security guarantees for Ukraine, warning that there was still reason to fear the new commitments could turn into another Budapest Memorandum or set of Minsk (I and II) Agreements. Signed in the past to protect Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty, these international agreements did not prevent Russia from attacking Crimea in 2014 and launching a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. "We must hope that these security guarantees, if they come from the US, are really serious and will also be implemented," said Reisner. Wilfried Jilge of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) also feared the current talks could lead to a "Minsk III." He warned against a "buffer zone" in Donbass, which Russians could access. Zelenskyy said after the talks in Berlin that the US had suggested setting up a "free economic zone" in the areas of the region currently controlled by Ukraine. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "As soon as the Russians are in such an area, even if it's just police forces, it's can be expected that regulations will be undermined and manipulated again," Jilge told DW. This could lead to "the Ukrainians being drawn into provocations again, which Russia will ultimately use to have another reason to occupy the area." More importantly, however, he pointed out that so far Russia had not said it was prepared to sign anything. The first statements from Russia after the talks in Berlin offer little hope for a swift agreement. The Kremlin rejected Chancellor Merz's idea of a short Christmas ceasefire. " We want peace — we don't want a truce that would give Ukraine a respite and prepare for the continuation of the war," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov. In response to a question about security guarantees, he said: "We have not seen any texts yet. Once we see them , we will analyze them." Russia's attacks on Ukraine are likely to continue over the holidays. This text was originally published in Ukrainian.

extraction.body: European leaders' commitment to security guarantees for Ukraine is important but not crucial, say experts. What about the US and Russia? One of the main topics of discussion in Berlin on December 14 and 15 was the post-ceasefire security guarantees that Ukraine would receive in the event of an agreement with Russia . In addition to European leaders, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, US special envoy Steve Witkoff, and Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump took part in the talks. Afterwards, there was a telephone call with the US president. At a joint press conference, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Zelenskyy were upbeat about the progress made. They said that there had been discussion of security guarantees akin to those offered by Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty and territorial questions. In their "Leader's statement on Ukraine," European leaders referred to a "European-led 'multinational force Ukraine' made up from contributions from willing nations." This would "assist in the regeneration of Ukraine's forces, in securing Ukraine's skies, and in supporting safer seas, including through operating inside Ukraine." The statement also outlined commitments in the event of peace to a " US led ceasefire monitoring and verification mechanism with international participation," as well as "a legally binding commitment, subject to national procedures, to take measures to restore peace and security in the case of a future armed attack" on Ukraine . Citing its own sources, the Reuters news agency reported that Zelenskyy had agreed during the talks in Berlin to drop Ukraine's NATO bid in return for security guarantees from the West. It remains unclear what the guarantees for Ukraine could look like in concrete terms. "These measures may include armed force, intelligence and logistical assistance, economic and diplomatic actions," the European leaders' statement said. So far, the US has not issued an official statement. According to the AFP news agency, a US official said that the "basis of the agreement is basically to have really, really strong guarantees — Article Five like — also a very, very strong deterrence." This reportedly did not involve the deployment of US troops. Susan Stewart from the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) told DW that the European leader statement and the fact that it outlined concrete measures was "very important" for Ukraine. She said that the potential security guarantees were similar to those granted to NATO members by Article 5 , which obliges the alliance to support a member state if it is attacked. "Article 5 of the NATO treaty does not stipulate that an attack must be responded to with military means, but rather that each state should must use the means it deems necessary and appropriate," she pointed out. Stewart said it would only be possibly to assess the guarantees thoroughly once all the details had been published. "But I think it's very important that this step has now been taken, to list these points and say: 'Yes, we as Europeans are ready to do this.'" She said that the statement indicated that "certain agreements with the US" had already been made. In the opinion of Claudia Major, a security expert at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, the security guarantees for Ukraine are not comparable to those granted NATO members. "It is support. However, it is not a legally binding obligation to defend Ukraine in the event of a new attack," she told German public broadcaster ARD. She said that on the basis of what is currently known there was no way of deducing what might happen concretely in the wake of a future Russian attack. "Will troops be sent? Will someone come to defend Ukraine, as would happen in NATO? This is not the case." He did not think that Russia would make concessions since it believes it is "on the path to victory," he said. "The specific issue here is Donbass, whether or not the Russians can effectively take possession of the entire region. At the moment, the Russians are insisting on this. Until this happens, Putin will continue this war. Reisner was also skeptical about the potential security guarantees for Ukraine, warning that there was still reason to fear the new commitments could turn into another Budapest Memorandum or set of Minsk (I and II) Agreements. Signed in the past to protect Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty, these international agreements did not prevent Russia from attacking Crimea in 2014 and launching a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. "We must hope that these security guarantees, if they come from the US, are really serious and will also be implemented," said Reisner. Wilfried Jilge of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) also feared the current talks could lead to a "Minsk III." He warned against a "buffer zone" in Donbass, which Russians could access. Zelenskyy said after the talks in Berlin that the US had suggested setting up a "free economic zone" in the areas of the region currently controlled by Ukraine. This could lead to "the Ukrainians being drawn into provocations again, which Russia will ultimately use to have another reason to occupy the area." More importantly, however, he pointed out that so far Russia had not said it was prepared to sign anything. The first statements from Russia after the talks in Berlin offer little hope for a swift agreement. The Kremlin rejected Chancellor Merz's idea of a short Christmas ceasefire. " We want peace — we don't want a truce that would give Ukraine a respite and prepare for the continuation of the war," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov. In response to a question about security guarantees, he said: "We have not seen any texts yet. Once we see them , we will analyze them." Russia's attacks on Ukraine are likely to continue over the holidays. This text was originally published in Ukrainian.

extraction.body: For the first time since February, Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. negotiators are scheduled to hold talks on ending the full-scale war that is nearing the five-year mark, with security guarantees topping the agenda. The two-day session starting Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, follows previous negotiations early this year that failed to produce any visible progress toward ending Europe's most devastating conflict since World War II. The talks follow last month's localized truce around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine that was brokered with the help of U.S. first lady Melania Trump and allowed the evacuation of some of its residents and the delivery of desperately needed humanitarian supplies. But even as Moscow and Kyiv touted the weeklong ceasefire as a positive model, fierce fighting has continued along the 750-mile front line. Both sides also have escalated their long-range attacks on each other with drones and missiles. Russia has intensified its strikes on Ukraine's power system, seeking to undermine the country's resolve as winter sets in. Moscow has relied on ballistic missiles and new, faster jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Ukraine's shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors. A look at the talks and what's on the agenda: Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on key elements of any prospective peace deal. Even after many of their smaller peers gave up over the past 12 months, the biggest digital asset treasury (DAT) companies are still buying Bitcoin ( BTC -1.73% ) and Ethereum ( ETH -5.31% ) . When they do, it means there are fewer coins available for everyone else who might want to buy them. In the week ending Nov. 1, Strategy ( MSTR -0.29% ) bought 811 BTC, and Bitmine Immersion Technologies ( BMNR -1.26% ) bought 8,573 ETH.
Their pace of buying is down to a trickle compared to a year ago, but for the coins themselves, that doesn't stop me from being bullish about how they'll perform. Here's why.

DAT companies sell their stock, preferred shares, or debt to the market to raise capital that they then use to buy and hold crypto. When the market caps of these crypto treasury stocks fall beneath the value of the coins on their balance sheets, that plan stops working, and they often need to sell. Per Bitwise Asset Management's October 2026 report, at least a dozen businesses that launched Bitcoin treasuries in 2025 have since sold every coin, mostly to repay debt or return cash to shareholders.
Even Strategy, the pioneer of this entire business model, had to sell some of its Bitcoin to cover its needs.

In its third-quarter earnings report, it said it had sold $431.8 million of Bitcoin this year so far to fund the preferred dividends associated with some of its classes of shares, and also to fund stock buybacks for some classes of its shares. Strategy holds a total of 849,327 BTC as of Nov. 5, or about 4% of Bitcoin's 21 million coin cap. So far, it's still a net buyer despite making some sales.

Because it was still buying, the available supply of newly mined Bitcoin wasn't large enough to make up for the demand. Bitcoin mining currently creates 450 BTC daily. Strategy's hoard grew by 83,901 BTC in the second quarter, which was 205% of miners' output in that period. In Q3, its net additions shrank to 1,666 BTC, or about 4% of new supply, per Cointelegraph's tally of company filings.
Now, think about that classic diagram in every economics textbook which shows how (in theory) the price of an asset changes based on how much supply is produced relative to demand.

Strategy's purchases don't change anything about Bitcoin's fundamental properties, like its supply limit or how much miners can produce. However, it isn't the only buyer, and it controls a meaningful slice of the supply already. That means as Bitcoin's mining reward declines over time as a result of its halving, new buyers will need to compete with each other to secure a slice of their own. That's bullish.

Unlike Bitcoin, Ethereum has no supply cap, which means that DAT companies have a higher bar to clear in terms of exerting supply pressure before their efforts have a chance to translate into higher prices for the coin.

At the Ethereum network's current level of activity, the coin's supply increases by around 0.8% annually, which is approximately 2,764 ETH created on a daily basis. The network pays those new coins to stakers, while part of each transaction fee on the blockchain is destroyed to prevent the increases to the circulating supply from diluting holders much.

As of Nov. 5, Bitmine, the largest Ethereum treasury company, held 6,060,506 ETH, or 4.9% of the supply, and has bought more each week since June 30, 2025. In the last week of October, its purchases were worth 44% of Ethereum's net new weekly supply.

For Ethereum, the reason to be bullish is that Bitmine and other DATs buying the coin is just one avenue for it to gain in value. As its network activity increases, more Ether will be burned, putting upward pressure on prices. With an entire ecosystem of decentralized finance (DeFi) projects, services, and tokens that provide value, the chain has quite a few different avenues for growing network activity and subsequently boosting the price of Ethereum. That variety is one reason it can anchor a well-balanced crypto portfolio alongside Bitcoin.
Some of those projects in the ecosystem will inevitably flare out or become irrelevant, but even that process constrains the available Ethereum for buyers.
So, it makes sense to bet on the coin over the long term.

When they do, it means there are fewer coins available for everyone else who might want to buy them. In the week ending Nov. 1, Strategy (NASDAQ: MSTR) bought 811 BTC, and Bitmine Immersion Technologies (NYSE: BMNR) bought 8,573 ETH. Their pace of buying is down to a trickle compared to a year ago, but for the coins themselves, that doesn't stop me from being bullish about how they'll perform. Here's why. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » DAT companies sell their stock, preferred shares, or debt to the market to raise capital that they then use to buy and hold crypto. When the market caps of these crypto treasury stocks fall beneath the value of the coins on their balance sheets, that plan stops working, and they often need to sell. Per Bitwise Asset Management's October 2026 report, at least a dozen businesses that launched Bitcoin treasuries in 2025 have since sold every coin, mostly to repay debt or return cash to shareholders. Even Strategy, the pioneer of this entire business model, had to sell some of its Bitcoin to cover its needs. In its third-quarter earnings report, it said it had sold $431.8 million of Bitcoin this year so far to fund the preferred dividends associated with some of its classes of shares, and also to fund stock buybacks for some classes of its shares. Strategy holds a total of 849,327 BTC as of Nov. 5, or about 4% of Bitcoin's 21 million coin cap. So far, it's still a net buyer despite making some sales. Because it was still buying, the available supply of newly mined Bitcoin wasn't large enough to make up for the demand. Bitcoin mining currently creates 450 BTC daily. Strategy's hoard grew by 83,901 BTC in the second quarter, which was 205% of miners' output in that period. In Q3, its net additions shrank to 1,666 BTC, or about 4% of new supply, per Cointelegraph's tally of company filings. Now, think about that classic diagram in every economics textbook which shows how (in theory) the price of an asset changes based on how much supply is produced relative to demand. Strategy's purchases don't change anything about Bitcoin's fundamental properties, like its supply limit or how much miners can produce. However, it isn't the only buyer, and it controls a meaningful slice of the supply already. That means as Bitcoin's mining reward declines over time as a result of its halving, new buyers will need to compete with each other to secure a slice of their own. That's bullish. Unlike Bitcoin, Ethereum has no supply cap, which means that DAT companies have a higher bar to clear in terms of exerting supply pressure before their efforts have a chance to translate into higher prices for the coin. At the Ethereum network's current level of activity, the coin's supply increases by around 0.8% annually, which is approximately 2,764 ETH created on a daily basis. The network pays those new coins to stakers, while part of each transaction fee on the blockchain is destroyed to prevent the increases to the circulating supply from diluting holders much. As of Nov. 5, Bitmine, the largest Ethereum treasury company, held 6,060,506 ETH, or 4.9% of the supply, and has bought more each week since June 30, 2025. In the last week of October, its purchases were worth 44% of Ethereum's net new weekly supply. As its network activity increases, more Ether will be burned, putting upward pressure on prices. With an entire ecosystem of decentralized finance (DeFi) projects, services, and tokens that provide value, the chain has quite a few different avenues for growing network activity and subsequently boosting the price of Ethereum. That variety is one reason it can anchor a well-balanced crypto portfolio alongside Bitcoin. Some of those projects in the ecosystem will inevitably flare out or become irrelevant, but even that process constrains the available Ethereum for buyers. So, it makes sense to bet on the coin over the long term. In Q3, its net additions shrank to 1,666 BTC, or about 4% of new supply, per Cointelegraph's tally of company filings.
Now, think about that classic diagram in every economics textbook which shows how (in theory) the price of an asset changes based on how much supply is produced relative to demand.

Strategy's purchases don't change anything about Bitcoin's fundamental properties, like its supply limit or how much miners can produce. However, it isn't the only buyer, and it controls a meaningful slice of the supply already. That means as Bitcoin's mining reward declines over time as a result of its halving, new buyers will need to compete with each other to secure a slice of their own. That's bullish.

Unlike Bitcoin, Ethereum has no supply cap, which means that DAT companies have a higher bar to clear in terms of exerting supply pressure before their efforts have a chance to translate into higher prices for the coin.

At the Ethereum network's current level of activity, the coin's supply increases by around 0.8% annually, which is approximately 2,764 ETH created on a daily basis. The network pays those new coins to stakers, while part of each transaction fee on the blockchain is destroyed to prevent the increases to the circulating supply from diluting holders much.

As of Nov. 5, Bitmine, the largest Ethereum treasury company, held 6,060,506 ETH, or 4.9% of the supply, and has bought more each week since June 30, 2025. In the last week of October, its purchases were worth 44% of Ethereum's net new weekly supply.

For Ethereum, the reason to be bullish is that Bitmine and other DATs buying the coin is just one avenue for it to gain in value. As its network activity increases, more Ether will be burned, putting upward pressure on prices. With an entire ecosystem of decentralized finance (DeFi) projects, services, and tokens that provide value, the chain has quite a few different avenues for growing network activity and subsequently boosting the price of Ethereum. That variety is one reason it can anchor a well-balanced crypto portfolio alongside Bitcoin.
Some of those projects in the ecosystem will inevitably flare out or become irrelevant, but even that process constrains the available Ethereum for buyers.
So, it makes sense to bet on the coin over the long term.

extraction.body: One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting an investigation. US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. On Sunday, Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. US tech giant Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the reports. The firm said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Huang was committed to continuing to lead the company. Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported. Her current whereabouts are unknown. Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked. However, the BBC understands Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking". It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. She did not respond to the paper's request for comment. When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not. "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us," an Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC. China has previously rejected the spying allegations, with a spokesperson saying that "the allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China". The New York Times reported in late October that Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf. Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he wished he had "acted on the intelligence", Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Huang. Last spring, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman, according to the New York Times. Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race , which is why the billionaire's affair has sparked national security fears among American lawmakers. Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way. Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China . He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang. "I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country". Founded by Huang and fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993, the company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games. Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates . Currently worth $4.5tn (£3.4tn), Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies ever. For now, the firm's board appears to have little appetite for removing Huang, saying in a statement on Sunday that they have "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team". Sources tell the BBC his removal is unlikely because there is so much money at stake. Brendan Mooney was speaking as Kainos announced a record half-year performance. Adoration for the US tech giant’s CEO Jensen Huang has been labelled “Jensanity”, but can his reputation survive the news of his affair? One prospective buyer says it is like going to buy a new Mercedes but ending up with an old Skoda.

extraction.body: MPs, local authorities, lawyers, schools and more are receiving floods of grievances, requests and legal challenges, often complex to read and respond to ‘I t started as a trickle in 2024 and now it’s an onslaught.” Hollie Wickens, a senior caseworker in a Labour MP’s office, is explaining the daily reality of dealing with surging volumes of artificial intelligence-generated correspondence. “Half the emails we receive are some form of AI,” she says, adding that this has made requests and complaints much more complex and time-consuming to read and deal with, despite her decade of experience in the role. “It is definitely more taxing.” At the start of this decade, applying for a job, writing a complaint or objecting to a local planning application typically required considerable effort: time to research a topic, fill in a form or write a formal-sounding email, with specialist knowledge often also required. The developers of AI tools promised huge productivity gains for employers and their staff: dull, routine tasks could be automated and carried out far more quickly, giving the human workforce more time for creative endeavours. There are signs of those gains in parts of the economy, with AI credited for some of this year’s better than expected UK GDP growth. However, UK businesses, local authorities, courts, schools and other public bodies are reporting being swamped by a flood of AI-generated complaints, letters and legal challenges that are massively increasing their workload , at a time of already stretched resources . This phenomenon has been called “AI clog” by commenters. With the concept of low-quality “AI slop” now mainstream, organisations are sounding the alarm that their operations are being gummed up by ever greater volumes of correspondence. These only take moments for users to create, but huge amounts of time for human employees to sift through and respond to. Bombarding public bodies with AI-generated requests has been labelled “agentic flooding” by researchers at the centre for digital governance at the Hertie School in Berlin, the Cooperative AI Foundation and GovAI. “Every sector is experiencing very similar issues,” says Deborah Evans, the chief executive of Lawyers in Local Government (LLG), an organisation that represents 5,600 lawyers working in local authorities. “Obviously AI is a wonderful tool that enables people to do things very, very quickly and it can make a complaint sound incredibly professional, very formal.” Local authorities are experiencing surging numbers of complaints, which can relate to issues from adult social care services to missed bin collections or objections to planning applications. “Local authorities have one pot of money and don’t get extra money because of more complaints,” Evans says. Local authorities believe the length of correspondence is an indication that it has been artificially generated, as does the inclusion of certain phrases or use of bullet points. “It’s a real problem,” says councillor Alessandro Georgiou, the leader of Enfield council. “More and more residents are using it to appeal decisions of the council, such as a significant uptick in parking appeals.” The information rights watchdog, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) , found that many public authorities received more requests in 2025. It noted that AI-generated requests can be “very long, repetitive and contain unrelated comments or misdirected demands”, have a greater scope, and be written in a way that makes it harder to identify what information is being requested. Before the widespread use of chatbots, the average length of complaints received by local authorities was about two pages. The majority are now 10 times longer, says Evans. “You get some huge ones. The worst one I’m aware of at the moment is about 200 pages long,” she says. Despite this, the ICO cautions that requests that appear to be drafted using AI and contain inaccuracies still need to be answered by humans. AI tools can often treat complaints as a legal claim, Evans says. “It will start referring to statute and pull out case law, but not necessarily tied to the jurisdictional boundaries in which you operate. It might find some great case law from Canada or somewhere. [AI] is also slightly prone to hallucinations so it does occasionally make things up.” Some business owners worry that AI’s tendency to be overly supportive and validating can give people misplaced confidence to pursue a legal case. “Everyone’s got a free lawyer now,” complains the founder of one technology start-up. One of its former employees, who was let go on performance grounds, is challenging their dismissal through an employment tribunal, although the entrepreneur insists the process was handled correctly. “You can tell by the wording [that the complaint is AI-generated] and it has a different tone.” Amid a long backlog of employment tribunal cases, the founder expects they will have spent £30,000 on legal fees by the time the case is heard. The founder’s experience is by no means unique, according to Jim Moore, an employee relations expert at Hamilton Nash. Many of his clients are receiving correspondence that is either entirely AI-generated or relies heavily on wording from AI tools. The complaints received by employers are described as “unnecessarily verbose” and containing “embellished or exaggerated claims that portray relatively minor incidents as major offences”. Moore says many AI-generated complaints “miss out on the most important point of a complaint – what resolution are you looking for? Most of the time, they’re worded to sound intimidating but forget to set out what solution the complainant wants.” The statutory response times for some requests are putting further pressure on public bodies clogged up by AI-generated correspondence. Transport for London (TfL), the public body responsible for the capital’s public transport system, received a record 4,769 freedom of information (FoI) requests in 2025-26, a 5% increase on the previous peak in 2023-24. The number of appeals sent to TfL is also rising, according to the minutes of a recent meeting of its audit and assurance committee. It reported a “noted increase” in appeals that appeared to be generated by AI “which often contain highly technical and often inaccurate assertions and assumptions”. The offices of some MPs are also struggling to cope. Vonnie Sandlan, the head of office for Graeme Downie, the Labour MP for Dunfermline and Dollar, says dealing with a surge in AI-generated requests has left her staff “exhausted”. “They are stretched to the limits and working more hours than they are paid,” she says. She notes that AI agents could aid those who would struggle to draft correspondence without help, but says her office has recently decided to stop responding to automated “click to email your MP” campaigns, to allow them to focus on constituents’ requests. The GMB union, which represents MPs’ office staff, has found soaring casework levels to be widespread. “AI is not lightening the load in MPs’ offices,” says Lisa Gillmore, the president of the MPs’ and peers’ staff branch. “Where offices keep their own figures, that casework has doubled or more and staff are carrying it with no let-up.” Evans warns that every pound spent by local authorities on dealing with complaints “is a pound that’s not being spent on something else, which is why getting things under control is important”. Some ombudsman services are now imposing word limits for complaints, she says, or designing online templates to restrict how much information can be attached. Others fear that organisations might start using AI tools to sift through AI-generated correspondence, with machine talking to machine. But this doesn’t come without cost and “losing the human touch”, as Evans puts it. Wiltshire council has said it is exploring using AI tools to summarise long emails and draft initial responses, while a committee at Stroud district council in Gloucestershire has discussed how it uses Microsoft’s Copilot to help with writing reports and presenting information. The UK government has issued civil servants with advice on using AI tools, including verifying facts provided, not inputting personal data and making sure humans review the work and take final decisions. The technology journalist Jamie Bartlett has been approached by many people sharing their experiences of AI clog. “Public bodies and companies are probably going to have to use some form of AI to start filtering things out, or set stricter rules on what they’ll accept and what they won’t,” he says. “Otherwise I worry they’re going to get completely overwhelmed.”

The developers of AI tools promised huge productivity gains for employers and their staff: dull, routine tasks could be automated and carried out far more quickly, giving the human workforce more time for creative endeavours. There are signs of those gains in parts of the economy, with AI credited for some of this year’s better than expected UK GDP growth. However, UK businesses, local authorities, courts, schools and other public bodies are reporting being swamped by a flood of AI-generated complaints, letters and legal challenges that are massively increasing their workload , at a time of already stretched resources . This phenomenon has been called “AI clog” by commenters. With the concept of low-quality “AI slop” now mainstream, organisations are sounding the alarm that their operations are being gummed up by ever greater volumes of correspondence. These only take moments for users to create, but huge amounts of time for human employees to sift through and respond to. Bombarding public bodies with AI-generated requests has been labelled “agentic flooding” by researchers at the centre for digital governance at the Hertie School in Berlin, the Cooperative AI Foundation and GovAI. “Every sector is experiencing very similar issues,” says Deborah Evans, the chief executive of Lawyers in Local Government (LLG), an organisation that represents 5,600 lawyers working in local authorities. “Obviously AI is a wonderful tool that enables people to do things very, very quickly and it can make a complaint sound incredibly professional, very formal.” Local authorities are experiencing surging numbers of complaints, which can relate to issues from adult social care services to missed bin collections or objections to planning applications. “Local authorities have one pot of money and don’t get extra money because of more complaints,” Evans says. Local authorities believe the length of correspondence is an indication that it has been artificially generated, as does the inclusion of certain phrases or use of bullet points. “It’s a real problem,” says councillor Alessandro Georgiou, the leader of Enfield council. “More and more residents are using it to appeal decisions of the council, such as a significant uptick in parking appeals.” The information rights watchdog, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) , found that many public authorities received more requests in 2025. It noted that AI-generated requests can be “very long, repetitive and contain unrelated comments or misdirected demands”, have a greater scope, and be written in a way that makes it harder to identify what information is being requested. Before the widespread use of chatbots, the average length of complaints received by local authorities was about two pages. The majority are now 10 times longer, says Evans. “You get some huge ones. The worst one I’m aware of at the moment is about 200 pages long,” she says. Despite this, the ICO cautions that requests that appear to be drafted using AI and contain inaccuracies still need to be answered by humans. AI tools can often treat complaints as a legal claim, Evans says. “It will start referring to statute and pull out case law, but not necessarily tied to the jurisdictional boundaries in which you operate. It might find some great case law from Canada or somewhere. [AI] is also slightly prone to hallucinations so it does occasionally make things up.” Some business owners worry that AI’s tendency to be overly supportive and validating can give people misplaced confidence to pursue a legal case. “Everyone’s got a free lawyer now,” complains the founder of one technology start-up. One of its former employees, who was let go on performance grounds, is challenging their dismissal through an employment tribunal, although the entrepreneur insists the process was handled correctly. “You can tell by the wording [that the complaint is AI-generated] and it has a different tone.” Amid a long backlog of employment tribunal cases, the founder expects they will have spent £30,000 on legal fees by the time the case is heard. The founder’s experience is by no means unique, according to Jim Moore, an employee relations expert at Hamilton Nash. Many of his clients are receiving correspondence that is either entirely AI-generated or relies heavily on wording from AI tools. The complaints received by employers are described as “unnecessarily verbose” and containing “embellished or exaggerated claims that portray relatively minor incidents as major offences”. Moore says many AI-generated complaints “miss out on the most important point of a complaint – what resolution are you looking for? Most of the time, they’re worded to sound intimidating but forget to set out what solution the complainant wants.” The statutory response times for some requests are putting further pressure on public bodies clogged up by AI-generated correspondence. Transport for London (TfL), the public body responsible for the capital’s public transport system, received a record 4,769 freedom of information (FoI) requests in 2025-26, a 5% increase on the previous peak in 2023-24. The number of appeals sent to TfL is also rising, according to the minutes of a recent meeting of its audit and assurance committee. It reported a “noted increase” in appeals that appeared to be generated by AI “which often contain highly technical and often inaccurate assertions and assumptions”. The offices of some MPs are also struggling to cope. Vonnie Sandlan, the head of office for Graeme Downie, the Labour MP for Dunfermline and Dollar, says dealing with a surge in AI-generated requests has left her staff “exhausted”. “They are stretched to the limits and working more hours than they are paid,” she says. She notes that AI agents could aid those who would struggle to draft correspondence without help, but says her office has recently decided to stop responding to automated “click to email your MP” campaigns, to allow them to focus on constituents’ requests. The GMB union, which represents MPs’ office staff, has found soaring casework levels to be widespread. “AI is not lightening the load in MPs’ offices,” says Lisa Gillmore, the president of the MPs’ and peers’ staff branch. “Where offices keep their own figures, that casework has doubled or more and staff are carrying it with no let-up.” Evans warns that every pound spent by local authorities on dealing with complaints “is a pound that’s not being spent on something else, which is why getting things under control is important”. Some ombudsman services are now imposing word limits for complaints, she says, or designing online templates to restrict how much information can be attached. Others fear that organisations might start using AI tools to sift through AI-generated correspondence, with machine talking to machine. But this doesn’t come without cost and “losing the human touch”, as Evans puts it. Wiltshire council has said it is exploring using AI tools to summarise long emails and draft initial responses, while a committee at Stroud district council in Gloucestershire has discussed how it uses Microsoft’s Copilot to help with writing reports and presenting information. The UK government has issued civil servants with advice on using AI tools, including verifying facts provided, not inputting personal data and making sure humans review the work and take final decisions. The technology journalist Jamie Bartlett has been approached by many people sharing their experiences of AI clog. “Public bodies and companies are probably going to have to use some form of AI to start filtering things out, or set stricter rules on what they’ll accept and what they won’t,” he says. “Otherwise I worry they’re going to get completely overwhelmed.”

sources.title: Apple is racing to make Siri more agentic
passages: Apple is expected to push Siri to become more agentic and enable features that will allow it to perform ongoing tasks, not just one-offs.

Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year — not that it has much of a choice, given current consumer and market demands.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says CEO John Ternus is pressuring AI czar Craig Federighi to accelerate the Siri roadmap and deliver a powerful AI agent that can compete with OpenAI’s Dots or Meta’s Muse.
Two significant improvements are expected to be made to Siri in the coming months.
One will give the assistant fine-grained control over Apple’s first-party apps, allowing it to do things like rotate and crop images in Photos and organize Safari tabs.
That would let Siri place an order through Grubhub or book a dinner reservation through OpenTable, for example.

sources.title: Meet Drops, the new music app bringing back the fun of sharing songs with friends
passages: The company says Drops is meant to feel like a return to how people used to discover music in the first place.
Before every platform’s algorithm recommendations, people often heard about new songs through friends, music blogs, or online communities.
Launched Monday by Harman , a Samsung subsidiary, Drops aims to make discovering new music feel social again.

“You send a friend a song and say, ‘You have to hear this.’ Then you end up texting, ‘Skip to 1:47, that’s the best part.’ The part that hits usually isn’t the first few seconds, and there wasn’t a good way to share just that moment,” Clare Hunter, general manager of Drops, told us.

extraction.body: Tesla CEO Elon Musk is defending the Cybertruck and the company’s decision to stop producing the polarizing steel-clad truck, claiming that the order rate far exceeds its production. Tesla will shut down production of the Cybertruck in about eight months Musk said in an X post on Monday. He also said the company will try to make as many of the vehicles as possible before then, though Tesla will “have to return deposits for a lot of people.” Musk argued the Cybertruck was not unprofitable, and that Tesla was ending production because the “opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.” In other words, Musk is arguing that Tesla can make more money by using the factory space and resources dedicated to the Cybertruck for building Cybercab robotaxis. Musk said last week that Tesla plans to use the factory space to build more two-seater Cybercabs. The first Cybertrucks were delivered to customers in late 2023, when it seemed like it could be a breakthrough hit for the company. Reservations for the vehicle had ballooned to 1 million, according to Musk , who also predicted that the company would sell around 250,000 of the trucks annually. But those reservations never translated into actual sales. Tesla doesn’t break out sales of the Cybertrucks, but industry experts estimate a total of about 71,000 Cybertrucks have been sold since the first deliveries began in November 2023. Many of those sales came from inside Musk’s ecosystem of other businesses. For instance, SpaceX (now known as SpaceXSI), which he also leads and is the largest shareholder of, purchased $131 million worth of Cybertrucks from Tesla in 2025, according to the company’s S-1 registration statement ahead of its IPO. Another Musk company, xAI, also bought $430 million worth of Tesla Megapacks for its data centers, before it merged with SpaceX. But sales of the Cybertruck, which lagged for months, could see a final bump now that it’s going out of production. Still, even a scarcity boost is unlikely to push the truck’s demand to the lofty projections from several years ago. extraction.body: Tesla CEO Elon Musk is defending the Cybertruck and the company’s decision to stop producing the polarizing steel-clad truck, claiming that the order rate far exceeds its production. Tesla will shut down production of the Cybertruck in about eight months Musk said in an X post on Monday. He also said the company will try to make as many of the vehicles as possible before then, though Tesla will “have to return deposits for a lot of people.” Musk argued the Cybertruck was not unprofitable, and that Tesla was ending production because the “opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.” In other words, Musk is arguing that Tesla can make more money by using the factory space and resources dedicated to the Cybertruck for building Cybercab robotaxis. Musk said last week that Tesla plans to use the factory space to build more two-seater Cybercabs. The first Cybertrucks were delivered to customers in late 2023, when it seemed like it could be a breakthrough hit for the company. Reservations for the vehicle had ballooned to 1 million, according to Musk , who also predicted that the company would sell around 250,000 of the trucks annually. But those reservations never translated into actual sales. Tesla doesn’t break out sales of the Cybertrucks, but industry experts estimate a total of about 71,000 Cybertrucks have been sold since the first deliveries began in November 2023. Many of those sales came from inside Musk’s ecosystem of other businesses. For instance, SpaceX (now known as SpaceXSI), which he also leads and is the largest shareholder of, purchased $131 million worth of Cybertrucks from Tesla in 2025, according to the company’s S-1 registration statement ahead of its IPO. Another Musk company, xAI, also bought $430 million worth of Tesla Megapacks for its data centers, before it merged with SpaceX. But sales of the Cybertruck, which lagged for months, could see a final bump now that it’s going out of production. Still, even a scarcity boost is unlikely to push the truck’s demand to the lofty projections from several years ago. extraction.body: “There’s no doubt that whatever it’s going to be called, it won’t be called Golden Dome.” Two of the top lawmakers backing the Pentagon’s Golden Dome missile defense shield are among the wave of Republicans leaving Congress in the coming Democratic takeover, raising questions about the future of President Donald Trump’s signature second-term defense initiative. The shakeup on Capitol Hill comes after military officials signaled in recent months that they might backpedal from one element Trump asked for in Golden Dome: the capability to shoot down missiles in their initial boost phase shortly after launch. The Golden Dome has escaped serious congressional scrutiny since Trump announced the program in January 2025, one week into his second term in the White House. That lack of scrutiny will change as Democrats take responsibility for writing the Pentagon’s budget, introduce limits on funding, and put forth bills to strip out Golden Dome’s most controversial component and give the program a new name. That’s the opinion of a half-dozen current and former officials in industry and government. Ars spoke with sources before and after last week’s congressional elections to get a sense of how a new Democratic Congress might make its imprint on missile defense. It’s important to know that much of what the Trump administration calls “Golden Dome” was already in development (or in some cases, operational) when Trump signed the executive order outlining the initiative 22 months ago. Trump’s order created a new program to consolidate the Pentagon’s existing missile defense efforts, accelerate work already underway on new Ground-Based Interceptors (GBIs), and deploy a new layer of orbiting sensors and Space-Based Interceptors (SBIs) to defend the US homeland against both traditional ballistic missiles and new emerging threats like drones and hypersonic weapons. The Golden Dome was immediately politicized. The first tranche of its funding —approximately $24 billion — was part of Trump’s so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill,” along with some of the White House’s other contentious policy priorities. The bill passed Congress on a party-line vote. This meant the budget for Golden Dome was not part of the normal military budgeting process in Congress, which usually involves both parties. Instead, it passed Congress through a controversial shortcut known as reconciliation . Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said in a September hearing that the White House’s decision to link Golden Dome’s first tranche of funding to a partisan reconciliation bill was unnecessary. “This should have been on a bipartisan basis,” Rounds said. Indeed, Capitol Hill Republicans refused the Trump administration’s effort to add $350 billion to the Pentagon’s budget this year through a similar reconciliation mechanism. Lawmakers also formed an all-Republican “Golden Dome Caucus” soon after the unveiling of Golden Dome. Seven House members of the caucus either lost their reelection bids or did not run for reelection at all in the 2026 midterms. These include the caucus’s co-chair, Rep. Jeff Crank (R-Colo.), and the chair of the House subcommittee overseeing Golden Dome, Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R-Tenn.). Both are among the Golden Dome’s biggest cheerleaders in Congress. The Democratic ranking member of the House Subcommittee on Strategic Forces, Rep. Scott Moulton (D-Mass.), is retiring from Congress. That leaves Rep. John Garamendi (D-Calif.) as the next-senior Democrat on the subcommittee, with a path to becoming chairman when the new Congress convenes in January. In remarks earlier this year, he called Golden Dome a “massive, extraordinarily expensive, and ultimately inadequate defensive system.” “When you use the words Golden Dome, now it’s political, and when you politicize national security, you get a political response, so it is damaging,” said John Plumb, who supervised military space policy for the Biden administration, in a panel discussion at the CyberSat conference this week. The Trump administration projects Golden Dome will cost $185 billion over the next 10 years, a figure that’s hard to verify with the scarce information military officials have released about how the system will work. Other cost estimates are significantly higher. The Congressional Budget Office concluded that a national missile defense system meeting the requirements set out in Trump’s executive order would cost about $1.2 trillion. The American Enterprise Institute released a report last year with a menu of potential Golden Dome architectures, ranging from a quarter-trillion dollars (without SBIs) to $3.6 trillion at the high end. Pentagon officials chafe at these numbers, claiming they do not take into account the military’s assumptions for low-cost launches and mass-produced satellite networks. But there’s more to the story than SBIs. The satellites and radars that detect and track missile launches are either in use today or were already in development during previous administrations. The same goes for Ground-Based Interceptors, which have been deployed for decades to take out missiles as they approach their targets. Under President Biden, the Pentagon’s Missile Defense Agency awarded Lockheed Martin a $17 billion contract to develop a next-generation Ground-Based Interceptor to defend against more sophisticated missile threats. The $24 billion Congress approved for Golden Dome last year was a one-time allocation for fiscal year 2026, which ended on October 1. The program’s funding dried up last month because the government is currently operating under a continuing resolution—an extension of last year’s regular military budget, which, of course, did not include the $24 billion Golden Dome infusion routed through reconciliation. The preliminary funding bills in the House and Senate for fiscal year 2027, if passed as-is, would provide only a fraction of the more than $17 billion the Trump administration requested for Golden Dome in this budget cycle. That’s because the Trump administration again separated a significant part of its record $1.5 trillion topline military budget request into a reconciliation package outside of the normal congressional appropriations process. The supplemental $350 billion funding request—which included funds for Golden Dome—went nowhere in the Republican-controlled Congress. And it won’t happen when Democrats take the gavels next year, either. It’s impossible to judge the realism of the Pentagon’s aim to get a first draft of Golden Dome up and running by the end 0f 2028, before the end of Trump’s presidency, because so much of the system is classified—but skepticism is the safer bet. Military officials have said little about Golden Dome’s design, architecture, or concept of operations, citing a national security imperative for secrecy. One thing we do know is that a homeland defense shield like Golden Dome will need international partners to host radar sensors, ground stations, and missile batteries. Canada is an obvious target for such a partnership, and a fully deployed Golden Dome would notionally provide protection over all of North America. However, this part of the program is off to a slow start. Michael Guetlein, the four-star Space Force general in charge of Golden Dome development, said earlier this year that tariffs—a core Trump administration policy—were limiting his interactions with foreign governments. So what can we expect when the next Congress convenes with Democratic majorities in January? The consensus among the experts Ars interviewed is that military leaders will still push for new options in missile defense, a need they say is underscored by their experience during the US war with Iran and Russia’s persistent missile strikes on Ukraine. Modern missiles and drones can easily dodge existing defense systems. The stark expense of existing Western interceptors compared to the cost of Iranian missiles and drones can make defenders think twice about whether to shoot or keep their powder dry for a future attack. So what do the people actually building Golden Dome think? Their answer is similar. Some missile defense priorities will survive, but maybe with a new name. The name Golden Dome is a “brand,” said Dylan Taylor, chairman and CEO of Voyager Technologies, which works with Anduril on SBIs. “It’s a proxy for layers of a protective onion, if you will, and there are elements of what is being called Golden Dome, where the technology is very advanced, and it works. The systems work. They’re more functional than I think people have reported on or have indicated.” “Golden Dome is a lot more than SBIs,” said another executive at a space company working on the project. “It’s one layer and element. We believe that there’s bipartisan support for this capability because it is a required capability for national security. The question is whether it can be achieved at a price that makes it executable and palatable. The technical aspect of this closes, and there’s just a question about scalability and cost.” The executive told Ars that newer, smaller space companies can do the job for less money than the Pentagon’s legacy contractors. Many companies are spending private capital on Golden Dome-related research and development with the promise of future Pentagon business. Military leaders have added stops on Wall Street and with venture capital firms to their usual tours of bases, command centers, and test ranges. “There’s real hardware being built by all the players,” the official said, suggesting optimism about fielding a working preliminary version of Golden Dome by 2028. “From us, on our execution to date, we’ve conducted engine tests and thermal tests and communications tests. “My fiduciary responsibility is to turn our investment into these critical technologies into future value, and I wouldn’t have made that call had I not been comfortable with the survivability of the program, assuming we can achieve the technical and financial targets, which we’ve convinced ourselves we can,” the official said. Rocket Lab is another company with business ties to Golden Dome. The company’s founder and CEO, Peter Beck, told Ars he was convinced missile defense will remain a priority no matter who controls Congress or the White House. “Is it a national security imperative that we go to the Moon? Probably not. Is it a national security imperative that we can protect the nation from incoming missile threats? Yes,” Beck said. “With these sorts of things, I’d say it’s what shape and scale they are, not whether they survive.” “There are elements of Golden Dome that I don’t think are going to be politically vulnerable, and there will be other parts of Golden Dome that, of course, will be,” Taylor said. “The point I want to emphasize is people who say, ‘Well, Golden Dome is dead; the whole thing is dead,’ they don’t necessarily understand that there are four or five or six layers to the system, and some are vulnerable and some are not.” Voyager’s expertise for missile defense is in advanced propulsion, and Taylor said those technologies are relevant for a range of systems, not just Golden Dome. “There’s no doubt that whatever it’s going to be called, it won’t be called Golden Dome, and there will definitely be machinations in the system, but it won’t be a ‘throw the baby out with the bath water’ approach,” Taylor said. “Given the risk profile, I don’t see that happening.” In a Senate hearing in September, Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, proposed the idea of a name change as one option to “depoliticize” the missile defense issue. “It is no secret that the ‘Golden Dome’ moniker has contributed to political polarization around the effort,” Karako said in his testimony. “Several options exist to depolarize and depoliticize the effort. It belongs to Congress to name or rename executive departments—witness the pending proposal to rename the Department of Defense as the Department of War.
